top5.why: The single best demand dossier in the field: a 6.0M-view video (Mar 2026) on a channel under 1 year old, a 1.98M-view video in 10 weeks on a second sub-2-year channel, both API-verified, plus a 1.72M-sub adjacent ceiling — recent, repeatable, multi-channel, broad-audience proof, married to the best RPM tier ($8-22 finance-adjacent). Main watch-out is the AI-slop crowd arriving in the same lane.

Edwards Economics (0 to 358k subs / 12.26M views in under 16 months, API-verified with full upload-playlist pagination) is the strongest single young-channel proof anywhere in the 28, backed by How Money Works' 1.72M ceiling and Wall Street Millennial's sustained 35-125k/video — proven current demand from a broad US audience plus top-tier finance monetization. Docked on sustainability for doom-fatigue and fast-follower risk since the template is visible to everyone.

Demand proven from multiple independent angles, all recent and API-verified: a 478k-view video (Apr 2026) on a 19-month-old channel, TWO near-identical Tenerife videos absorbing 248k and 108k views weeks apart (demand exceeds supply), a 1.44M-sub ceiling, and even a hyperlocal 6.4k-sub channel with 950k views. Evergreen bottomless well and clean policy posture make this the safest demand bet.

Three concurrent mid-size faceless channels (286k/24.4M, 278k/57.6M, 395k adjacent) prove the audience sustains multiple sellers, and the decisive skeptic evidence is a brand-new entrant: Waterline Salvage, created 2025-11-25, at 831k views on 14 videos in 7 months. Add a professional-mariner core plus casual disaster viewers (breadth), monthly new official reports, and near-zero fad risk.

Format demand is explosive and freshly proven at the newcomer level — a 947k-view video from a channel created 6 weeks earlier (Dec 2025), a 2.79M-view video in 6 weeks, 151M views on 80 JokeLore videos — with high browse/viral ceiling. Ranked fifth rather than higher because every proof point is medieval Europe; the pitch's non-medieval eras carry unproven demand (the researcher labels it inference), so treat era expansion as a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

commentary: From a proven-viewing-behavior standpoint this field is sharply bimodal. The history, money, and disaster-forensics lanes carry genuinely excellent evidence — recent (2026) API-verified view counts, multiple independent channels, and crucially young/small channels outperforming their subscriber counts (Dr. Jonathan Tam, Edwards Economics, DisastersUncovered, Waterline Salvage, George's History, Ditlev Gren). That is the gold standard: breadth, recency, and repeatability. The weakest candidates lean on exactly what I punish. C28 is the clearest overreach: its researcher verified only that nobody occupies the lane — whitespace is not demand, and an empty lane after a decade of YouTube language-learning may mean the demand isn't there in this format. C19 substitutes a case PIPELINE (news stories, a podcast, an ISOGG index) for any YouTube view count in the actual format — zero video-level demand proof. C27's own API pull contradicts its thesis (legit senior-health channels at 221 and 438 subs while misinfo farms take the 3.3M views); the 19x/21x growth multipliers cited for C25/C27 come from TubeLab/OutlierKit vendor snippets that were 403-blocked and never even read in full — they should carry no weight. C02's demand is media-giant one-offs (Business Insider 7.8M) plus a single High Yield outlier; no dedicated channel of any age has proven the recurring beat, which its own researcher concedes. C05 is a launch-window spike on a game whose concurrents are down 22% and still below its 12-year-old predecessor. C26 and C04 both borrow demand from generic AI-news channels while proposing a profession-niched version whose closest real test (accountant videos at 966-17k views) is a negative signal. On overrating by their own researchers: C20's 'explosive unit economics' belong to incumbents in the most saturated lane presented, C15's headline numbers come from a senator's channel and CNBC (institutional reach, not organic niche demand), and C12's enormous demand is real but sits inside a genre YouTube is actively pressured to demote — the researcher was right to call it highest-risk. Finally, the vidIQ faceless-breakout scan deserves a warning label: it is dominated by Shorts compilations, reused-clip farms, and meme edits — near-zero overlap with any gate-passing candidate — and mainly confirms that the low-effort end of faceless YouTube is saturated slop, which strengthens the case for the research-moat candidates at the top of my ranking. Note also C09 and C17 tie at 7.35; I'd break the tie toward C09 on audience breadth and lower incumbent count in its long-tail territory.
